chapter: New York 1930s and New Orleans expatriates
title: Forgotten names, Fazola and Eddie Miller's low clarinet
summary: Kmen forgets names, then discusses Fazola with Crosby and Eddie Miller's low-register clarinet chorus.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: Did you know Elma and Nicholas, a clarinet player? Danny Gawka, a guitar player? They used to be around the taproom. At least they made some records with Rolini during that period. Well, there were two things that happened here.

First of all, there were so many musicians that you met. That union floor and the street around the union floor after union hours was just loaded with musicians and you don't remember, you know, you just didn't get their name or associate with them. And then the other thing that operates is the fact that I've forgotten a lot of the fellows' names. I've tried to recall in my own mind sometimes, many of the people that I work with, I can remember their face and the fact that I'm working with them better than I can remember their name. And in some cases I know I never will remember the name unless it's brought to my attention. I don't know.
Well, what about, say, Tony Almarico, was he up there for them? That period I'm trying to remember, or did you know him?
I guess he made trips up there, but I've only read this from later. I didn't meet him up there or know of him up there.
What about Fazzola? Did you know him?

Oh yes, everybody's in Fazzola. Just everybody. Fazzola came on the scene with the Bob Crosby band shortly after Goodman had generated all this interest in clarinet, and it was just a solid rave all the way, Fazzola's clarinet playing. And there again you have an example, because prior to that time, well, Eddie Miller played some clarinet, made one notable recording instead of fashion of clarinet, and then wasn't it Matty Matlock that played clarinet with that band too? Yeah. I remember when Fazzola came in, he was the king in that band.
What was the Miller record? Do you remember? It might sometime, Dick.

There was one low register clarinet thing that's become almost a standard, sort of like Bix's chorus on Birth and the Blues, one of these things that's a set of pattern. And much to my surprise upon it was Eddie Miller that had recorded that. It's in one of the standard big band, Dixieland numbers, like Muscat Ramble or Rampage Street, some of that, that's lots of numbers. And Miller, once we played that low, Newman clarinet chorus on it. Right in that shallow, move range of the clarinet, and big sonorous tone down there, and never getting up into the upper range.
Yeah, and that was kind of out of fashion then, wasn't it?

Well, it became a kind of characteristic of Dixieland. Often you see when they come to the trio and the Dixieland number that followed that form, the first clarinet chorus in that trio would be down in that register. And then the second one would move up more into the upper register.
